verdict: Over the lab's stated need of at least 6 years, buy the sequencer. Confidence is moderate. Over the 48-month lease term alone, on a like-for-like basis at 8%/12 per month with end-of-month flows, the lease is cheaper by only about $4,958 in present value. Lease PV is about $471,062 and buy PV is about $476,020, a gap of roughly 1%. That 48-month result is fragile. It reverses if the month-48 resale is above about $96,821 or if the right discount rate is below about 7.53% per year. It also assumes the lab sells the instrument at month 48, which the lab does not plan to do. The lab needs 6 or more years, and the lease ends at month 48 with no purchase option. Buying and keeping the instrument for 72 months costs about $565,552 in PV even if it is worth nothing at year 6. For leasing to match that, all replacement equipment and service for months 49-72 would have to cost less than about $94,490 in PV, which is about $5,879/month. That is roughly half the current $11,500 lease rate. Re-leasing at the same rate would cost about $90,345 more in PV than buying and keeping. The controller memo's premise is false. The lease totals $552,000 nominal, not about $480,000. The buy option nets $462,000 nominal after service and resale. The lease carries an implied financing rate of about 7.53%, so it is not 'free financing'. The recommendation to buy depends on four conditions: (a) service for months 49-72 costs about $1,500/month (this is not quoted); (b) the lab has no binding capital constraint (unknown); (c) the tax-ignored scope is appropriate (unknown); and (d) the lab accepts the obsolescence risk of owning the platform through year 6. Confirm these with the vendor and finance before committing.

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Recomputed from the verified quote inputs (E1, E2) and the finance convention (E3). Over 48 months the lease is cheaper in PV by about $4,958 (K8): lease $471,062 (K6) against buy $476,020 (K7). This confirms the researcher's hand figures (E6) to within about $6. E6 gave a lease PV of about $471,056, and the exact formula gives $471,062. The margin is about 1% of either total, so it is not a decisive win for the lease.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: This comparison assumes the lease's 'included' service is equivalent to the $1,500/month purchase-side service contract. The quote does not confirm this (E2), so it is an unverified assumption, not a fact. Under that assumption both options carry the same 48-month service stream, and the comparison reduces to financing: $480,000 now, less the PV of a $90,000 residual, against $10,000/month of net lease payments. At 8% the residual's PV is only 0.72692 per dollar (K4). The lease's $10,000/month annuity (factor 40.9619, K5) is worth slightly less than the net outlay for buying. In effect, and again only under the service-equivalence assumption, the lessor prices the financing at about 7.53% (K12), just under the lab's 8%.
strengths: All inputs come from VERIFIED documents (vendor quote, finance assumptions).
The formulas are standard and reproducible in a spreadsheet: PV(0.08/12,48,-11500) gives 471,062.
Independent recomputation matches the researcher's hand figures closely.
weaknesses: The result assumes the lease's 'included' service matches the $1,500/month contract in scope. The quote does not say (E2).
It assumes the vendor's $90,000 resale is achieved (E1, E10).
It ignores possible end-of-lease return costs (E13) and installation or insurance costs, none of which are in the quote.

criteriaAssessments.assessment: The 6-year horizon decides the question and favours buying. The lab needs at least 6 years (E3). The lease has no purchase option and the equipment goes back at month 48 (E2). Buying and keeping the instrument for 72 months, with $1,500/month service throughout and no year-6 resale, costs PV $565,552 (K15). Leasing for months 1-48 costs $471,062, so any lease-side solution for months 49-72 must cost less than $94,490 in PV (K16), or about $5,879/month level (K17), just to break even. A same-rate re-lease would cost $655,897 in total (K18), which is $90,345 more than buy-and-keep (K19). On an equivalent-annual-cost basis (E14), buy-and-keep costs about $9,916/month (K21), against $11,500/month for the lease. Over 48 months buying costs about $11,621/month (K20), so the instrument's longer service life is what makes buying cheaper.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Most of the purchase cost is front-loaded and sunk. Years 5-6 of ownership cost only service, plus the forgone month-48 resale. A lease charges the full rate for each period of use. Once the needed horizon runs past the lease term, the owner's marginal cost for months 49-72 (about $1,500/month service plus the forgone resale) is far below any plausible replacement lease.
strengths: The breakeven framing ($94,490 PV, or $5,879/month) needs no assumption about unknown re-lease terms. The CFO only has to judge whether a replacement could plausibly cost less than half the current rate.
The advantage holds even with zero year-6 resale. Any positive resale R widens it by 0.61977 x R (K14).
weaknesses: Service pricing for months 49-72 is not quoted. With a sole-source OEM (E12), the price could escalate.
No source gives re-lease or replacement terms (E8 limitations).
A replacement at month 48 would probably be a newer platform with lower running costs (E11), so lease-plus-replacement is not strictly like-for-like with keeping a 4-year-old instrument.

criteriaAssessments.assessment: The memo's premises are wrong on its own arithmetic and on economics. 11,500 x 48 = $552,000 (K1), not about $480,000. Nominal net buy cost is $462,000 (K2), so on undiscounted totals the lease costs $90,000 more (K3). The memo also leaves out the $72,000 of purchase-side service, the $90,000 resale and the time value of money. The lease is not 'free financing'. Its implied rate is about 7.53% per year (K10-K12), far above 0%. On a correct PV basis the 48-month lease is marginally cheaper, but for a different reason than the memo gives, and the margin is too small to call it an 'easy yes'.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: The memo compares a nominal sum of lease payments, which it also miscomputes, against the bare purchase price. That mixes timing, leaves out the service the lease bundles in, and drops the residual value the buyer keeps.
strengths: The correction is simple arithmetic on VERIFIED inputs and anyone can reproduce it.
weaknesses: The memo's 'preserves cash' point is valid in principle, but only if a capital constraint exists, and that is unknown (E16).

criteriaAssessments.assessment: The 48-month result is fragile and the 72-month result is robust. Over 48 months buying wins if resale exceeds about $96,821 (K9), only about 7.6% above the vendor's $90,000, or if a single discount rate applied to all flows is below about 7.53% (K12). E9 says the textbook lease-vs-buy rate is the secured borrowing rate, which is often below a cost-of-capital figure, so a lower borrowing rate would push the 48-month result toward buying. The same framework, however, discounts the uncertain $90,000 residual at a higher, risk-adjusted rate. E10 and E11 show that residual is highly uncertain, so a risk-adjusted rate would lower its PV and widen the lease's 48-month edge. The two adjustments pull in opposite directions, and their net effect is not quantified here, so the 48-month winner cannot be called either way with confidence. Each $1,000 change in resale moves the buy PV by about $727. At a $60,000 resale the buy PV rises to about $497,828 (K23) and the lease wins the 48-month comparison by about $26.8k. $60,000 is mid-range among the E10 asking prices, not a low case: those listings run from GBP 8,000 (a spares unit) and $42,250 up to EUR 200,000. They are also asking prices for a different instrument (NovaSeq 6000) whose original price may differ from $480k, so they are not scaled to this unit, and a much lower resale than $60,000 is plausible. Over 72 months the buy-and-keep advantage over a same-rate re-lease is about $90k (K19). That is far larger than any of these input swings, unless service escalation in years 5-6 is extreme or replacement equipment is far cheaper.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Over 48 months the PV of the resale (about $65.4k) is about 13 times the PV gap (about $5k), so small resale errors, or the rate used to discount the resale, change the outcome. The implied lease rate sits next to the 8% hurdle, so the choice of discount rate also changes it. Over 72 months the buyer avoids roughly two years of full lease payments, which outweighs resale and rate effects.
strengths: The breakevens are explicit and checkable (K9, K10-K12, K16-K17).
weaknesses: Service escalation could not be quantified because no price data was found (E12).
The implied-rate breakeven is bracketed and interpolated between 7.5% and 7.6%, not solved exactly. A spreadsheet RATE/IRR should confirm it.
The offsetting effects of a lower borrowing rate and a risk-adjusted residual rate are described qualitatively, not computed.
E10 resale data are unscaled asking prices for a different instrument, so the resale downside as a share of the $480k cost may be larger than the $60k case suggests.

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Mixed, and this is the main argument for leasing. Platform generations turn over quickly. A successor cut cost per Gb by up to 60% and is not chemistry-compatible, and a provider phased out the prior platform (E11, by analogy). The lease passes residual and obsolescence risk to the vendor. Its exit is expensive, though: 70% of remaining payments, so $193,200 to exit at month 24 (K22, E15). It gives no ownership and may carry return or refurbishment costs (E13). Buying keeps the residual risk (E10 shows widely spread used prices) but allows resale at any time without a termination penalty.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: With a lease, the vendor prices in its own residual forecast. With a purchase, the lab bears the variance of the residual. Fast technology turnover lowers residuals and raises the value of being able to upgrade. However, the lease's termination clause blocks cheap mid-term upgrades, so its flexibility advantage is mostly limited to the month-48 exit.
strengths: The termination exposure is computed directly from the verified quote terms.
weaknesses: The obsolescence evidence concerns a real comparable platform, not the fictional Corvid S4, and rests on snippets (E11).
Return-condition terms for this lease are unstated (E13 is general guidance).

criteriaAssessments.assessment: Cannot be determined from the packet. The lease avoids a $480,000 upfront outflow. That matters beyond the 8% discount rate only if the lab faces a real capital or liquidity constraint, and no information on this exists (E16). Without a constraint, PV already prices the timing difference, so 'preserves cash' adds nothing.
criteriaAssessments.mechanisms: Discounting at the cost of capital already charges for tying up cash. Cash timing deserves separate weight only under capital rationing, for example a capped capital budget or a covenant.
strengths: The criterion is framed correctly as secondary to PV.
weaknesses: The lab's capital position is entirely unknown (E16).

claims.text: Over 48 months at 8%/12 monthly with end-of-month flows, lease PV is about $471,062 and buy PV (with $90,000 resale) is about $476,020. The lease is cheaper by about $4,958, roughly 1%.
The controller memo's arithmetic is wrong. Lease payments total $552,000, not about $480,000. On nominal totals the buy nets $462,000, so the lease costs $90,000 more undiscounted.

The lease is not free financing. Assuming its included service is equivalent to the $1,500/month purchase-side contract (unverified; the quote does not say, E2), its implied rate is about 7.53% per year: buy-minus-lease PV is about -$320 at 7.5% and about +$742 at 7.6%.
The 48-month result flips to buying if month-48 resale exceeds about $96,821 or if a single discount rate applied to all flows is below about 7.53%.

Over 72 months, buying and keeping the instrument costs PV about $565,552 with zero year-6 resale, assuming $1,500/month service continues. A lease-side replacement for months 49-72 would need to cost less than about $94,490 PV (about $5,879/month) to match. A same-rate re-lease costs about $90,345 more than buy-and-keep.
On an equivalent-monthly-cost basis, buy-and-keep over 72 months costs about $9,916/month (zero resale), against $11,500/month for the lease. Over 48 months buying costs about $11,621/month.
Early termination of the lease is costly. Exiting at month 24 would cost $193,200 (70% of $276,000 remaining).

The $90,000 resale is an unbacked vendor estimate. Used units of a comparable-class but different instrument are listed at widely varying asking prices, from GBP 8,000 (spares) and about $42k-$60k up to EUR 200k. These are not scaled to this instrument's $480k price. At a $60,000 resale, which is mid-range in that data rather than a low case, the 48-month buy PV rises to about $497,828.
Service pricing for months 49-72 and any escalation cannot be determined from the evidence. The OEM may be the sole service provider, which creates escalation risk for the buy-and-keep path.

Whether the lab faces a capital or liquidity constraint, or is tax-exempt, cannot be determined from the evidence. Either could change the weight of the 'preserves cash' argument or the after-tax result.
Fast platform turnover in this equipment class, shown by analogy to NovaSeq 6000 and NovaSeq X, raises obsolescence and residual-value risk for an owner keeping the instrument through year 6.

Standard lease-vs-buy practice discounts the lease-related flows at the secured borrowing rate rather than the cost of capital. The packet does not say whether the stated 8% is a borrowing rate or WACC. A lower borrowing rate would favour buying over 48 months, but the same framework discounts the risky residual at a higher, risk-adjusted rate, which would favour leasing. The net effect is not quantified here.

A negotiated month-48 purchase option would make leasing match buy-and-keep only if priced below about $70,381 in PV, which is about $96,821 payable at month 48. That is because the lab would still pay about $24,109 PV of service for months 49-72. The threshold equals the 48-month resale breakeven.

alternatives.option: Buy and sell at month 48 (the quote's base case)
alternatives.comparison: PV $476,020 against lease $471,062 over 48 months (K6, K7). This is about $4,958 worse than leasing, but it does not cover the 6-year need, so it is mainly a benchmark.

alternatives.option: Buy and keep to year 6 or later
alternatives.comparison: PV about $565,552 less 0.61977 x the year-6 resale (K15, K14). This is the recommended path. It is about $90,345 cheaper than a same-rate re-lease (K19), and it beats any lease-side continuation that costs more than about $5,879/month for months 49-72 (K17).

alternatives.option: Lease 48 months, then re-lease or lease a successor platform for months 49-72
alternatives.comparison: At the same $11,500/month the total PV is about $655,897 (K18). This only beats buy-and-keep if the continuation costs below about $94,490 PV (K16). It does provide a newer platform from month 49.

alternatives.option: Lease 48 months, then buy a successor at month 48
alternatives.comparison: This cannot be priced from the packet because no successor price is available. The successor's purchase price plus its months 49-72 service, less the PV of any year-6 resale credit, would need a PV below about $94,490 (K16) to match buy-and-keep. If successor service also costs $1,500/month (PV about $24,109, K25), the purchase price would need a PV below about $70,381 (K24), or about $96,821 paid at month 48 (K9), plus any resale credit. That is implausible for a new instrument when this one costs $480,000.

alternatives.option: Negotiate the lease (add a purchase option or lower the rate)
alternatives.comparison: A lease rate low enough that the 48-month plus continuation cost beats buy-and-keep would require a large concession. A month-48 purchase option would make leasing match buy-and-keep only if priced below about $70,381 in PV (K24), about $96,821 payable at month 48 (K9). This is because the lab would still pay about $24,109 PV of service for months 49-72 after exercising it (K25). The threshold equals the 48-month resale breakeven, as it should. Use it as a ceiling, not a target. Any option price above about $96.8k leaves buy-and-keep cheaper.

tradeoffs: Buying costs less in PV over the 6-year need but puts $480,000 up front and leaves the lab holding residual and obsolescence risk.
Leasing transfers residual risk and gives a natural upgrade point at month 48, but costs more over 6 years and is very expensive to exit early (70% of remaining payments).
Over 48 months alone the lease is about $5k cheaper in PV, but that margin is smaller than plausible errors in the resale value or discount rate.
Owning locks the lab into a sole-source service relationship whose price after month 48 is unknown. The lease locks the service price for 48 months.
edgeCasesAndFailureModes: Service escalation in years 5-6. If the post-warranty service price rises sharply under a sole-source OEM (E12), the buy-and-keep advantage shrinks. It would take roughly $90k of extra PV over months 49-72 to erase the advantage over a same-rate re-lease.

The platform becomes obsolete before year 6 (E11). The lab might want to replace the instrument at month 48 anyway, which brings the 48-month comparison back into play, where the lease is marginally cheaper.
Resale collapses. If used-market prices fall to scrap levels (E10 shows a GBP 8,000 spares unit), the 48-month buy PV rises by about $727 per $1,000 of shortfall.
The lease's 'included' service is narrower than the $1,500/month contract, for example in parts or uptime guarantees. Then the lease is not like-for-like and its effective cost is understated.
End-of-lease return, crating, shipping or refurbishment charges (E13) are not modelled and would erode the lease's roughly $5k 48-month edge.
Mid-term exit. A need to switch platforms at month 24 would trigger a $193,200 termination fee (K22), while the owner could simply sell.

Payment timing. Lease payments in advance rather than arrears would raise the lease PV by about 0.67% (roughly $3.1k). That would cut the 48-month gap to about $1.8k, roughly a third of its original size, without reversing it. The quote says arrears (E2), so this applies only if the contract differs.

counterarguments.argument: At the CFO's stated 8% rate the lease is cheaper, so the analysis should recommend the lease.
counterarguments.response: That holds only over 48 months and only if the instrument is sold at month 48. The lab needs at least 6 years and the lease has no purchase option, so the like-for-like comparison has to cover months 49-72. There, buying wins unless replacement costs less than about $5,879/month.

PV at 8% already charges for tying up that cash. Cash preservation deserves extra weight only under a binding capital constraint, and the packet has no information on one (E16). If such a constraint exists, it should be stated and quantified, for example as a higher hurdle rate. It should not be assumed.

counterarguments.argument: Owning a sequencer through year 6 is risky because technology moves fast and a newer platform may be far cheaper per Gb.
counterarguments.response: This is the strongest case for leasing (E11). However, the lease does not avoid the problem for months 1-48 because of the costly termination clause. After month 48 the lab can still sell the owned unit and upgrade. The rational comparison at month 48 is then the remaining owned-instrument cost against the new-platform cost, a decision the owner keeps and the lessee also has.

counterarguments.argument: The vendor's $90,000 resale may be optimistic, so buying is worse than shown.
counterarguments.response: That is true for the 48-month comparison (K23). But in the recommended buy-and-keep scenario the month-48 resale is not realised, and the 72-month advantage was computed with zero year-6 resale. So resale optimism does not undermine the 6-year recommendation.

correctedUserAssumptions.correction: Lease payments total $552,000 (11,500 x 48). The buy nets $462,000 nominal after $72,000 of service and $90,000 of resale, so the lease costs $90,000 more undiscounted. On a PV basis the lease is about $4,958 cheaper over 48 months only.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: The lease is 'effectively free financing' and 'an easy yes'.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: The lease's implied financing rate is about 7.53% per year, not 0%. The 48-month PV advantage is about 1% and flips with modest changes in resale or discount rate. Over the 6-year need, buying is materially cheaper.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: 8% cost of capital is the right discount rate.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: Standard lease-vs-buy practice discounts the lease-related flows at the secured borrowing rate. If one rate below about 7.53% is applied to all flows, buying wins even over 48 months. The same framework, though, discounts the uncertain residual at a higher, risk-adjusted rate, which would favour the lease over 48 months. The packet does not say whether 8% is a borrowing rate or WACC, so the net effect over 48 months is unresolved. It does not change the 72-month result.

correctedUserAssumptions.assumption: A 48-month comparison is the right horizon.
correctedUserAssumptions.correction: The lab needs at least 6 years and the lease has no purchase option, so a 72-month (or equivalent-annual-cost) comparison is required, and it favours buying.

practicalImplications: Recommend buying, provided the vendor confirms the post-warranty service price for years 5-6 in writing (ideally capped) and finance confirms there is no binding capital constraint.

Withdraw the controller memo's 'same total, free financing' rationale. The correct statement is that the 48-month lease is marginally cheaper at an implied rate of about 7.53%, and costlier over the 6-year need.

Ask finance whether 8% is the secured borrowing rate. If a borrowing rate below about 7.53% is applied to all flows, buying also wins over 48 months. Discounting the risky residual at a higher, risk-adjusted rate would pull the other way, so the 48-month result stays uncertain. The 72-month result favours buying either way.

If the lab still prefers to lease for obsolescence reasons, negotiate a month-48 purchase option priced below about $96,821 at month 48 (K9, K24), or renewal terms below about $5,879/month including service (K17). Get return-condition terms in writing before signing.
remainingUncertainty: Service price and scope for months 49-72 are unquoted, and the OEM may be the sole provider (E12).
Re-lease or replacement terms for months 49-72 are unknown. The 72-month comparison is a breakeven analysis, not a priced comparison.

The month-48 and year-6 resale values are not validated. E10 conflicts with the vendor's E1 figure, and the conflict is unresolved: E1 is the vendor's own unbacked estimate, and E10 consists of asking prices for a different, real instrument of unknown age and possibly different original price. Neither is authoritative, so resale is treated as a sensitivity input.
Whether the lease's 'included' service equals the $1,500/month contract in scope (E2). The like-for-like financing reduction and the 7.53% implied rate depend on this assumption.
The net effect of using a secured borrowing rate for lease flows and a higher risk-adjusted rate for the residual is not quantified, because the packet gives neither rate.
The lab's tax status and capital constraints (E16). If the lab is taxable, depreciation and lease deductibility could change the result.
The implied lease rate (about 7.53%) is interpolated, not solved exactly. A spreadsheet RATE should confirm it.
The researcher's E6 lease PV ($471,056) differs from the exact formula value ($471,062) by about $6. The recomputed figures here supersede it, and the difference does not change any conclusion.
furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion: A written vendor quote for service pricing in years 5-6 and its escalation terms. A very large escalation would narrow or reverse the buy-and-keep advantage.
Vendor renewal or re-lease terms, or a successor-platform price, for months 49-72. A continuation below about $5,879/month including service would favour leasing.

Confirmation of the lab's secured borrowing rate and an appropriate risk-adjusted rate for the residual. A single rate below about 7.53% favours buying over 48 months; a higher residual rate favours leasing over 48 months.
Evidence of a binding capital budget limit that would justify weighting the upfront $480,000 beyond PV.

Corvid S4 roadmap or end-of-support dates. If the platform will be obsolete well before year 6, the lab may replace at month 48 anyway, which makes the 48-month comparison (lease marginally cheaper) the relevant one.
Transaction-price data for 4-year-old instruments of this class, to firm up the resale value.
